Reward-Aligned Distillation

Yilan Chen1, Zian Su2,†\dagger Manish Prajapat3 Dingmin Wang3 Rui Song4     Rein Houthooft3     Vijay Lingam3,
1UC San Diego   2Purdue University   3AWS AI Labs   4Amazon ††thanks: Work done during an internship at AWS AI Labs. Yilan Chen: yic031@ucsd.edu; Zian Su: su284@purdue.edu.††thanks: Corresponding author: Vijay Lingam, vlingam@amazon.com.
Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but remains computationally expensive and sample inefficient. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, yet standard OPD distills every token regardless of whether the teacher’s preference actually improves task reward. Existing token-selection methods rely on proxies such as uncertainty or teacher–student divergence, which need not identify reward-improving supervision. We introduce Reward-Aligned Distillation (RAD), a bilevel framework that weights distillation signals based on their predicted effect on the student’s post-update reward. RAD differentiates through a temporary optimizer step to score each token’s supervision, then updates the token weights by projected ascent from the initial token weights. The resulting weights can strengthen, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions. At a matched training-response budget, RAD improves mean accuracy on six competition-math benchmarks over the strongest baselines by 6.5 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and 2.5 points for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. RAD-Simple, a simplified variant, achieves comparable math accuracy at the same training-response budget. On LiveCodeBench-v6, RAD reaches 54.69% and 58.67% pass@1 with Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and OLMo3-7B-Instruct, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by 8.7 and 6.4 points. These results support reward-guided weighting of teacher supervision across model families and tasks.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has been shown effective for improving mathematical reasoning (Luong and Lockhart, 2025) and code generation (Jaech et al., 2024; Ekbote et al., 2025) abilities, but its supervision is sparse: a long response often receives only a single sequence-level reward (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). On-policy distillation offers a complementary signal by evaluating student-generated responses under a strong teacher and supplying dense token-level guidance (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). This approach is appealing because the student continues to explore on policy while learning from the teacher at every generated token.

Standard OPD, however, implicitly treats the teacher as the target policy and every teacher preference as worth imitating. This would be justified if the teacher were optimal for the target reward, but a stronger teacher need not be reward-optimal. Teacher–student differences may reflect style, formatting, verbosity, or reasoning choices that do not improve task reward (Armandpour et al., 2026). Consequently, reducing teacher–student divergence does not guarantee reward improvement: uniform distillation can spend capacity matching reward-irrelevant behavior or move the student away from reward-improving solutions (Xu et al., 2026; Akhondzadeh et al., 2026).

The challenge is therefore to determine which teacher signals will benefit the student’s task performance. Token-selection methods (Xu et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026) use heuristic criteria such as uncertainty, teacher–student disagreement, and reasoning structure to selectively apply teacher supervision. These criteria identify potentially useful tokens, but do not directly assess whether the corresponding distillation update improves the student policy’s task reward. We therefore seek to choose each token’s distillation weight based on its predicted effect on reward: retain teacher signals that help the student solve the task, and suppress or reverse those that hinder it.

To this end, we introduce reward-aligned distillation (RAD), which weights teacher supervision by its predicted effect on task reward. Token weights affect reward indirectly, by controlling how the student learns from teacher supervision. RAD captures this dependency with a bilevel objective: the inner problem trains the student with weighted distillation, while the outer problem selects weights to maximize the trained student’s reward (Equation 2). We approximate the inner optimization with one temporary optimizer step using token weights initialized to a tunable value. Differentiating the temporary student’s reward with respect to these weights yields look-ahead scores that guide a projected ascent update. The resulting signed weights can strengthen, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions.

2 Related Work

On-policy distillation for LLMs. On-policy distillation queries a teacher on student-generated responses, reducing the training–inference mismatch of offline distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). Related self-distillation methods obtain teacher signals from the student itself using privileged information such as verified solutions or environment feedback (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026).
Unifying distillation and RLVR. KDRL (Xu et al., 2025) & RLAD (Zhang et al., 2026) combine verifiable rewards with teacher guidance, while RG-OPD (Akhondzadeh et al., 2026) uses verifier outcomes and teacher likelihoods to gate trajectory-level distillation. ExOPD (Yang et al., 2026) scales implicit teacher-derived rewards relative to KL regularization.
Token-selective distillation. TIP (Xu et al., 2026) selects tokens using uncertainty and teacher–student divergence, while DEAR (Xiao et al., 2026) identifies decision tokens and supporting evidence. Reopold (Ko et al., 2026) combines teacher-derived reward clipping with entropy-guided token sampling. Armandpour et al. (2026) develop an offline diagnostic of reward–distillation alignment, estimating token-level QQ-values by repeatedly sampling continuations after selected next-token choices, which is computationally expensive. They measure cosine similarity between local logit gradients and study oracle filtering of positively aligned tokens. RAD formulates token weighting as a bilevel optimization problem. A one-step approximation yields the sensitivity of post-update reward to each token’s weight, expressed as parameter-space alignment between its distillation gradient and an optimizer-adjusted reward direction. We estimate the reward gradient from minibatch rollouts, avoiding explicit branchwise QQ-value estimation. Both the sign and magnitude of the resulting scores guide projected ascent on bounded, signed weights, which strengthen, suppress, or reverse distillation contributions during training. We compare against representative baselines from both reward-aware and token-selective distillation literature. Extended related work appears in Appendix B.

3 Background

Let 𝒙∼𝒟\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D} denote a prompt sampled from the data distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}. We condition on 𝒙\bm{x} and omit its outer expectation throughout for simplicity. Let π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}} denote the student model, 𝒚=(y1,…,yT)∼π𝜽(⋅∣𝒙)\bm{y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T})\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid\bm{x}) be a response sampled from the student, and st=(𝒙,y<t)s_{t}=(\bm{x},y_{<t}) be the autoregressive state.

3.1 Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a policy to maximize rewards from verifiable outcomes, such as correct answers or passing code tests. Given a reward function R⁡(𝒙,𝒚)R(\bm{x},\bm{y}), the expected-reward objective is defined as:

JR(𝜽)=𝔼𝒚∼π𝜽(⋅∣𝒙)[R(𝒙,𝒚)].J_{R}(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{y}\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid\bm{x})}\left[R(\bm{x},\bm{y})\right].

Several policy-gradient surrogates can be used to optimize this objective in RLVR, including proximal policy optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) and group relative policy optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024). In this work, we use GRPO’s group-relative advantages to estimate the reward gradient. For each prompt, we sample GG responses {𝒚i}i=1G\{\bm{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from the student and normalize their rewards within the group: AiR=R⁡(𝒙,𝒚i)−μRσR,μR=1G​∑j=1GR⁡(𝒙,𝒚j),A_{i}^{R}=\frac{R(\bm{x},\bm{y}_{i})-\mu_{R}}{\sigma_{R}},\mu_{R}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}R(\bm{x},\bm{y}_{j}), where σR\sigma_{R} is the group reward standard deviation. Every token in 𝒚i\bm{y}_{i} receives the same response-level advantage AiRA_{i}^{R}.

3.2 On-Policy Distillation

On-policy distillation (OPD) samples responses from the student and evaluates the teacher on the same student-generated states (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). For a fixed teacher πT\pi_{\mathrm{T}}, the reverse-KL objective is defined as:

LD(𝜽)=𝔼𝒚∼π𝜽(⋅∣𝒙)[∑t=1Tlogπ𝜽​(yt∣st)πT​(yt∣st)].L_{D}(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{y}\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid\bm{x})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\frac{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})}\right].

Unlike GRPO’s sequence-level reward, OPD provides dense supervision at every generated token. Standard OPD, however, weights all token-level teacher signals equally. Moreover, minimizing LDL_{D} alone provides no monotonic improvement guarantee for JRJ_{R}.

4 Reward-Aligned Distillation

Reward-Aligned Distillation (RAD) selects token-level distillation weights according to their predicted effect on task reward. We introduce the weighted objective (§4.1), then develop a bilevel formulation and its one-step approximation (§4.2). We extend the resulting scores to general optimizers and compute them efficiently using Jacobian–vector products (§4.3). Algorithm 1 summarizes our training recipe. Finally, we present RAD-Simple, a simplified variant using pre-update reward gradients and shared distillation rollouts (§4.5).

4.1 Token-Weighted Distillation

Let πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}} denote the sampling policy. Holding sampled prefixes fixed, we define the per-token distillation surrogate

ℓD,t​(𝜽,𝒚)=π𝜽​(yt∣st)πold​(yt∣st)​log⁡π𝜽​(yt∣st)πT​(yt∣st).\ell_{D,t}(\bm{\theta};\bm{y})=\frac{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})}\log\frac{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})}.

Assigning real-valued token weights 𝒘⁡(𝒚)=(w1​(𝒚),…,wT​(𝒚))\bm{w}(\bm{y})=(w_{1}(\bm{y}),\ldots,w_{T}(\bm{y})), with prompt dependence suppressed, gives the weighted objective

LD(𝜽,𝒘)=𝔼𝒚∼πold(⋅∣𝒙)[∑t=1Twt(𝒚)ℓD,t(𝜽;𝒚)].L_{D}(\bm{\theta},\bm{w})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{y}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(\cdot\mid\bm{x})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}(\bm{y})\ell_{D,t}(\bm{\theta};\bm{y})\right]. (1)

The weights can strengthen, suppress, or reverse individual distillation contributions. Uniform weights wt=1w_{t}=1 recover the fixed-prefix OPD surrogate. Appendix F derives the corresponding gradient.

4.2 Bilevel Token Weighting

Recall that our goal is to choose token weights in order to maximize the reward after distillation. This naturally leads to a bilevel optimization formulation:

max𝒘⁡JR​(𝜽⋆​(𝒘))s.t.𝜽⋆​(𝒘)∈arg​min𝜽⁡LD​(𝜽,𝐰).\max_{\bm{w}}\;J_{R}\!\left(\bm{\theta}^{\star}(\bm{w})\right)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bm{\theta}^{\star}(\bm{w})\in\argmin_{\bm{\theta}}L_{D}(\bm{\theta},\bm{w}). (2)

The inner problem trains the student with weighted distillation, and the outer problem chooses weights to maximize the trained student’s reward. Solving the inner problem for each weight update is computationally infeasible. Therefore, we approximate its solution with one SGD (Robbins and Monro, 1951) update from the current student, with learning rate η>0\eta>0:

𝜽⋆​(𝒘)≈𝜽+​(𝒘)=𝜽−η​∇𝜽LD​(𝜽,𝒘).\bm{\theta}^{\star}(\bm{w})\approx\bm{\theta}^{+}(\bm{w})=\bm{\theta}-\eta\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}L_{D}(\bm{\theta},\bm{w}). (3)

At each iteration, we set the initial token weights wt(0)=cw_{t}^{(0)}=c for every token and denote the temporary student 𝜽+=𝜽+​(c​𝟏)\bm{\theta}^{+}=\bm{\theta}^{+}(c\mathbf{1}). For the sampled objective, differentiating the post-update reward through Equation 3 with respect to each token’s weight gives the token score, omitting the loss normalization:

∂JR​(𝜽+​(𝒘))∂wt​(𝒚)|𝒘=c​𝟏=−η⁡⟨∇𝜽+JR​(𝜽+),∇𝜽ℓD,t​(𝜽,𝒚)⟩≕It​(𝒚).\left.\frac{\partial J_{R}(\bm{\theta}^{+}(\bm{w}))}{\partial w_{t}(\bm{y})}\right|_{\bm{w}=c\mathbf{1}}=-\eta\left\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}^{+}}J_{R}(\bm{\theta}^{+}),\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\ell_{D,t}(\bm{\theta};\bm{y})\right\rangle\eqqcolon I_{t}(\bm{y}). (4)

A positive token score favors increasing the token’s weight, while a negative score favors decreasing it. We update the weights by one projected ascent step:

wt​(𝒚)=Π[c−1,c+1]​(c+γ​It​(𝒚)),γ>0.w_{t}(\bm{y})=\Pi_{[c-1,c+1]}\!\left(c+\gamma I_{t}(\bm{y})\right),\qquad\gamma>0. (5)

Π\Pi clips to the weights to be inside [c−1,c+1][c-1,c+1] to prevent extreme outlier values and γ\gamma is the weight learning rate. We will discuss the choice of initial weight cc in the next section. We reset the weights to cc for each new iteration, discard the temporary update, and train the original student with the updated weights. Figure 2 summarizes the iteration.

4.3 Optimizer-Aware Scoring via Jacobian–Vector Product (JVP)

We now extend the SGD derivation to general optimizers, including AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), which is widely used in LLM training. This extension accounts for how the student optimizer transforms the weighted distillation gradient. Let 𝒜⁡(𝜽,𝒈)\mathcal{A}(\bm{\theta},\boldsymbol{g}) denote the parameters returned by one optimizer step with gradient 𝒈\boldsymbol{g}, treating the pre-step optimizer state as fixed. Define 𝒈⁡(𝒘)=∇𝜽LD​(𝜽,𝒘)\boldsymbol{g}(\bm{w})=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}L_{D}(\bm{\theta},\bm{w}). The one-step approximation becomes

max𝒘⁡JR​(𝜽+​(𝒘))s.t.𝜽+​(𝒘)=𝒜⁡(𝜽,𝒈⁡(𝒘)).\max_{\bm{w}}\;J_{R}\!\left(\bm{\theta}^{+}(\bm{w})\right)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bm{\theta}^{+}(\bm{w})=\mathcal{A}(\bm{\theta},\boldsymbol{g}(\bm{w})).

We evaluate the token-weight derivatives at 𝒘=c​𝟏\bm{w}=c\mathbf{1}, writing 𝒈=𝒈⁡(c​𝟏)\boldsymbol{g}=\boldsymbol{g}(c\mathbf{1}) and 𝜽+=𝜽+​(c​𝟏)\bm{\theta}^{+}=\bm{\theta}^{+}(c\mathbf{1}). Similar to Equation 4, differentiating the post-update reward through this optimizer step gives the optimizer-aware token score,

It​(𝒚)=−⟨∇𝜽ℓD,t​(𝜽,𝒚),𝒑⟩,𝒑=−(∂𝒜⁡(𝜽,𝒈)∂𝒈)⊤​∇𝜽+JR​(𝜽+).I_{t}(\bm{y})=-\left\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\ell_{D,t}(\bm{\theta};\bm{y}),\boldsymbol{p}\right\rangle,\qquad\boldsymbol{p}=-\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{A}(\bm{\theta},\boldsymbol{g})}{\partial\boldsymbol{g}}\right)^{\!\top}\nabla_{\bm{\theta}^{+}}J_{R}(\bm{\theta}^{+}). (6)

For SGD, 𝒑=η​∇𝜽+JR​(𝜽+)\boldsymbol{p}=\eta\nabla_{\bm{\theta}^{+}}J_{R}(\bm{\theta}^{+}), recovering Equation 4. At c=0c=0, the distillation gradient vanishes, so plain SGD without momentum or weight decay gives 𝜽+=𝜽\bm{\theta}^{+}=\bm{\theta}. AdamW can still move through its existing moments and decoupled weight decay; token-weight derivatives can remain nonzero in either case. For AdamW, we differentiate through the moment updates and gradient clipping; the derivation is in Appendix G. Let ℓD\boldsymbol{\ell}_{D} collect the per-token surrogates. We compute all scores together using one JVP:

𝐈⁡(𝒚)=−JVP𝜽⁡[ℓD​(𝜽,𝒚)]​[𝒑]∈ℝ|𝒚|.\mathbf{I}(\bm{y})=-\operatorname{JVP}_{\bm{\theta}}[\boldsymbol{\ell}_{D}(\bm{\theta};\bm{y})][\boldsymbol{p}]\in\mathbb{R}^{\left\lvert\bm{y}\right\rvert}. (7)

The AdamW-specialized JVP is given in Equation 13. We implement a custom Triton kernel for the flash attention JVP; Appendix H gives the derivation and pseudocode (Algorithm 2).

Choice of initial token weight. The initial token weight cc determines both the temporary distillation update and the starting point for projected ascent. Under the symmetric constraint [c−1,c+1][c-1,c+1], c=1c=1 starts from uniform weights and learns a weight perturbation around 1 within [0,2][0,2], while c=0c=0 starts from zero weights and permits signed weights in [−1,1][-1,1]. We treat cc as a hyperparameter that may vary between iterations. Appendix A.3 compares these initialization choices. Experiments indicate that c=0c=0 learns slower than c=1c=1 but can achieve better final performance. Gradually expanding the negative range from [0,1]\,[0,1]\, to [−1,1]\,[-1,1]\, for c=0c=0 can help balance learning speed and performance.

4.4 RAD Training Algorithm

Distillation rollouts are used to update the student, whereas meta rollouts are used to estimate the reward gradient for token weighting. Both prompt batches are sampled from the same training dataset.

RAD’s bilevel formulation makes token weighting depend on the student’s post-update reward, introducing additional computation before each weighted distillation update. At each step, we take a temporary AdamW step with initial token weights c​𝟏c\mathbf{1}, generate separate meta rollouts, and estimate the reward gradient using GRPO objective. We compute the optimizer-aware token scores via a JVP (Equation 7), update the weights with Equation 5, and train the original student with the updated weights. The meta batch is only used to learn the token weights; the committed student update uses the distillation rollouts. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure of RAD, and Appendix A.2 gives the batch objective and implementation details. RAD can in principle combine any differentiable token-level OPD objective with any RLVR gradient estimator. Section 6.3 demonstrates compatibility with the OPD2 (Heo et al., 2026) distillation signal.

4.5 RAD-Simple: A Simplified Variant of RAD

The bilevel formulation adds a temporary optimizer update, meta rollouts, a reward-gradient computation, and a JVP to standard OPD. To simplify token scoring, RAD-Simple estimates the pre-update reward gradient by reusing the distillation rollouts. Replacing the post-update reward gradient in Equation 4 by the pre-update reward gradient gives

It​(𝒚)=−⟨∇𝜽JR​(𝜽),∇𝜽ℓD,t​(𝜽,𝒚)⟩.I_{t}(\bm{y})=-\left\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J_{R}(\bm{\theta}),\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\ell_{D,t}(\bm{\theta};\bm{y})\right\rangle.

We omit the common factor η\eta, which can be absorbed into the weight learning rate γ\gamma, and use the same projected weight update in Equation 5. RAD-Simple also omits the optimizer Jacobian, while the student update still uses AdamW. Reusing the distillation rollouts avoids the temporary student update and separate meta rollout generation, halving the number of training responses per step. The only additional computation compared with OPD are reward-gradient estimation and a JVP. RAD-Simple ignores changes in the reward gradient after distillation and the optimizer’s effect on token scores. Table 1 compares RAD-Simple with RAD at a matched training-response budget.

5 Experiments

We describe the experimental setup and evaluation protocol, then present math and coding results. Implementation details, including inference hyperparameters, appear in Appendix A.

5.1 Experimental Settings

We evaluate RAD on mathematical reasoning and code generation, and additionally evaluate RAD-Simple on mathematical reasoning.

Models. For mathematical reasoning, we use Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 as the teacher and Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as students (Yang et al., 2025). For code generation, we evaluate Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) with the same teacher, and OLMo3-7B-Instruct with OLMo3.1-32B-Instruct as its teacher.

Training protocol. We train with verl (Sheng et al., 2025) using 64 prompts and eight responses per prompt. Within each domain and student setting, all methods share the training data, student initialization, rollout group size, sampling configuration, and optimizer settings. RAD additionally samples an equally sized, separate meta batch from the temporary student and updates token weights using exact JVPs. We compare 100 RAD updates with 200 baseline updates, matching the generated training responses, including RAD’s meta rollouts. At this budget, RAD uses 17–18% more training time than OPD and RLAD on Qwen3-1.7B math, but less than TIP and ExOPD. On OLMo3-7B coding, RAD uses 18–39% less training time than the reported baselines (Table 11). RAD uses the initial token weight c=0c=0 in the main math and coding comparisons, with an additional cosine schedule of negative range for coding. Shared and method-specific settings appear in Appendix A.1.

Baselines. We compare RAD and RAD-Simple with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), OPD (Agarwal et al., 2024), TIP (Xu et al., 2026), RLAD (Zhang et al., 2026), and ExOPD (Yang et al., 2026). Given the higher training cost of the OLMo3-7B setting (Table 11), we retain GRPO and OPD as reference methods, with TIP and RLAD representing strongest token-selective and reward-aware distillation baselines, respectively. Baseline-specific hyperparameters follow the respective papers.

Mathematical reasoning. Following ExOPD (Yang et al., 2026), we train on 57,046 problems from DeepMath-103K (He et al., 2025) with difficulty ratings of at least 6. We evaluate on AIME24 (AI-MO, 2024), AIME25 (OpenCompass, 2025), AIME26, HMMT2025-Feb, HMMT2025-Nov (Balunovic et al., 2025), and OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024). We sample 16 responses per problem at temperature 1.0 and top-pp 1.0, with a 32,768-token generation limit. Responses are graded with Math-Verify 11 1 https://github.com/huggingface/Math-Verify, and pass@1 is estimated as the fraction of sampled responses that are correct. The overall score is the unweighted mean across the six benchmarks.

Code generation. We train on the Eurus code split (Cui et al., 2025), assigning reward 1 when all tests pass and 0 otherwise. We evaluate on all 1,055 LiveCodeBench-v6 tasks (Jain et al., 2025a). Following ExOPD (Yang et al., 2026), we sample four responses per task at temperature 1.0 and top-pp 1.0, with a 32,768-token generation limit. Dataset statistics appear in Table 5.

5.2 Mathematical Reasoning Results

At the matched training-response budget (Table 1), RAD reaches 39.07% mean accuracy with Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking), exceeding the strongest baseline, ExOPD at 32.59%, by 6.48 points. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, RAD reaches 59.80%, exceeding the strongest baseline, GRPO at 57.29%, by 2.51 points. The corresponding gains over OPD are 8.01 and 6.71 points. Figure 3 tracks both students on four benchmarks (AIME24/25 and HMMT2025-Feb/Nov). For the 1.7B student, RAD improves more slowly early in training but continues to improve as the distillation baselines plateau or decline. For the 4B student, RAD exceeds all baselines from step 30 onward. RAD-Simple trails RAD at 100 updates for both students but continues to improve, reaching comparable accuracy at 200 updates.

At the same training-response budget, RAD-Simple reaches 38.42±1.70%38.42\pm 1.70\% and 60.84±1.50%60.84\pm 1.50\% mean accuracy after 200 updates for the 1.7B and 4B students, respectively (Table 1). These results are 0.65 points below and 1.04 points above RAD at step 100, respectively, and exceed the strongest baselines by 5.83 and 3.55 points. This shows that the simpler pre-update scores can also support effective token weighting. However, within the same 100 training steps, RAD-Simple learns slower than RAD as shown in Figure 3. RAD-Simple removes the temporary optimizer update and separate meta rollouts, and computes token scores using the current-policy reward gradient without the optimizer Jacobian. It achieves similar math accuracy at a matched generated-response budget, but requires more training time for Qwen3-1.7B. This trade-off supports the practical value of RAD’s full scoring procedure: additional computation for estimating token weights can improve overall training efficiency.

For Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, OPD reaches 53.09% at step 200, slightly above the base student’s 52.38%, while TIP, RLAD, and ExOPD perform below the base student. Similar degradation of OPD and ExOPD is observed in Heo et al. (2026) (Table 4 and 5). RAD’s gain in this setting supports using post-update reward to guide the contribution of each teacher signal even when the initial teacher–student gap is small.

Appendix E.3 additionally compares RAD with baselines with a matched training time. Figure 10 in Appendix E.4 compares RAD at step 90 with GRPO at step 450 on math and coding, with GRPO using 2.5×\times as many generated training responses. Appendix E compares total training times for Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) on math and OLMo3-7B-Instruct on coding, and reports a RAD training-time breakdown for Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking).

5.3 Code Generation Results

Figure 4 compares both students across varying difficulty tiers on full LiveCodeBench-v6. Appendix C.1 reports the full numerical results (Table 8). RAD with Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) reaches 54.69±0.31\bf 54.69\pm 0.31% pass@1 at step 100, compared with 45.97±0.2645.97\pm 0.26% for RLAD, the strongest step-200 baseline. RAD also leads the five evaluated baselines on Easy, Medium, and Hard. Appendix C.2 reports Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) coding-validation dynamics and checkpoint results.

With OLMo3-7B-Instruct, RAD reaches 58.67±0.52\bf 58.67\pm 0.52% on full LiveCodeBench-v6 at step 100, exceeding GRPO at 52.27±0.2652.27\pm 0.26%, the strongest completed step-200 baseline, by 6.40 points. These results extend the coding comparison to a different model family and a larger student. Appendix C.3 reports OLMo3-7B-Instruct coding-validation dynamics and checkpoint results.

Preliminary experiments also extend RAD to agentic software engineering. On SWE-bench Verified, RAD achieves 50.5% pass@1, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.7 percentage points while training for half as many epochs (Appendix D).

6 Analysis and Extensions

In this section, we examine which components drive RAD’s performance, how token reweighting affects gradient alignment, and whether RAD extends to other distillation signals.

6.1 RQ1: Which components contribute to RAD’s performance?

We ablate RAD using Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) with c=0c=0 after 100 updates on AIME24/25 and HMMT2025-Feb/Nov (Table 2). Reversing scores or shuffling weights reduces accuracy from 32.71% to 0.36% and 6.35%, respectively, supporting token-specific alignment. Restricting weights to [0,1][0,1] yields 25.00%, while gradually introducing negative weights achieves 31.20%. Replacing AdamW lookahead with SGD yields 16.88%. These comparisons support signed weights and optimizer-aware scoring in this setting.

Evaluating the reward gradient before the temporary update achieves 34.32%, comparable to RAD. However, it achieves 47.19% compared with 55.26% of RAD for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, showing the benefit depends on the student setting. Reusing distillation rollouts further reduces accuracy to 18.54%, but also halves the generated responses per update. We next examine how token reweighting changes gradient alignment in RAD and RAD-Simple.

6.2 RQ2: Does token reweighting improve gradient alignment?

We compare uniform weights 𝒘=𝟏\bm{w}=\mathbf{1} and learned token weights at fixed Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) math checkpoints at steps 0 and 100. We measure cosine alignment between distillation descent direction (negative distillation gradient), −∇𝜽LD​(𝜽,𝒘)-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}L_{D}(\bm{\theta},\bm{w}), and RAD’s optimizer-aware reward direction 𝒑\boldsymbol{p} (Equation 6), and current student’s reward direction ∇𝜽JR​(𝜽)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J_{R}(\bm{\theta}).

Table 4 shows that reweighting increases cosine with 𝒑\boldsymbol{p} for RAD and ∇𝜽JR​(𝜽)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J_{R}(\bm{\theta}) for RAD-Simple at both checkpoints. RAD’s cosine with ∇𝜽JR​(𝜽)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J_{R}(\bm{\theta}) decreases: RAD’s token weights target the optimizer-aware reward direction 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}, which accounts for how changes in the distillation gradient affect post-update reward, rather than the immediate reward gradient.

6.3 RQ3: Is RAD compatible with other distillation signals?

We apply RAD’s token weighting to OPD2 (Heo et al., 2026), which derives supervision from an instruction-tuned teacher and its paired base model. We evaluate on the same four math benchmarks; implementation details appear in Appendix A.1.

Table 4 compares OPD2 + RAD after 100 updates with uniform OPD and OPD2 after 200 updates, matching the number of generated training responses. Adding RAD improves OPD2, supporting its compatibility with an alternative distillation signal. For Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, the combined method also approaches teacher accuracy (Figure 5).

7 Conclusion and Future Work

RAD uses optimizer-aware lookahead scores and projected ascent to align token-level distillation with reward. It improves math and coding accuracy at a matched training-response budget. Results with OLMo3-7B-Instruct extend the evidence to a different model family and a larger student, while OPD2 results support compatibility with other distillation signals. RAD-Simple reuses distillation rollouts and removes the temporary update; it improves over the strongest math baselines for both Qwen students at the same training-response budget, demonstrating the effectiveness of simpler token scoring in these settings.

Limitations and future work. RAD requires a temporary student update, fresh outer rollouts, and an exact JVP, increasing its per-step cost relative to standard OPD. RAD-Simple removes the temporary update and fresh outer rollouts but still requires reward-gradient estimation and a JVP. Further reducing these costs and understanding when optimizer-aware lookahead is beneficial remain important directions. Future work should explore longer training horizons, and learned or non-verifiable rewards.

Appendix A Experimental Details and Additional Math Results

A.1 Training Settings

Shared training setup. The reported main math and coding experiments use eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Each update uses 64 actor prompts with eight responses per prompt; RAD additionally samples 64 separate meta prompts with eight responses each. Tables 6 and 7 summarize the shared and method-specific math hyperparameters. We describe the datasets first, followed by the baseline implementations and RAD weight settings.

Math datasets and evaluation. Dataset sizes and evaluation metrics are listed in Table 5. For AIME26, we use the 30-problem MathArena snapshot with two upstream-confirmed transcription corrections. For OlympiadBench, we use the 675-problem Qwen2.5-Math evaluation snapshot.

Coding data. The Eurus code split is assembled from APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021), CodeContests (Li et al., 2022), Codeforces (Codeforces, ), and TACO (Li et al., 2023). The coding results in Tables 8, 9 and 10 use 25,276 training examples and 1,024 validation examples (Table 5).

Coding evaluation. LiveCodeBench-v6 contains 322 easy, 383 medium, and 350 hard tasks. Evaluation uses a 40,960-token context limit for the combined prompt and response, with at most 32,768 generated tokens per response. The main coding comparison reports RAD at step 100 and baselines at step 200.

Baseline implementations. GRPO optimizes task reward without teacher guidance, while OPD applies reverse-KL distillation uniformly to all response tokens. TIP uses Soft-OR selection with 50% token retention. RLAD modifies the clipped GRPO update with a teacher-aware policy ratio. ExOPD constructs a reward-extrapolated reverse-KL advantage using frozen student and teacher base policies. OPD, RLAD, ExOPD, and RAD use sampled-action estimates of reverse KL, while TIP uses full-vocabulary reverse KL as in their paper.

RAD weight settings. For the math and coding experiments, RAD uses distillation coefficient λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 to prevent excessively frequent gradient clipping, and weight learning rate γ=104​N1/N\gamma=10^{4}N_{1}/N in Equation 5. Here N1N_{1} and NN are the numbers of valid response tokens in the first and current actor batches, respectively. The unprojected weight change is γ​It\gamma I_{t}: the score ItI_{t} already includes the optimizer learning rate through the optimizer Jacobian and the scaling of the estimated outer reward gradient. The weight learning rate should therefore be interpreted together with this score scale; the resulting weights are clipped to the specified interval. We apply no further weight normalization. Both math runs use the fixed initial token weight c=0c=0 and clipping interval [−1,1][-1,1]. These are experimental settings, while Equation 5 keeps cc configurable. For RAD-Simple on math, we use λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 and γ=3​N1/N\gamma=3N_{1}/N for both Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. Both use c=0c=0 and clipping interval [−1,1][-1,1] throughout 200 updates.

The Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) coding RAD run uses the same weight learning rate γ=104​N1/N\gamma=10^{4}N_{1}/N with distillation coefficient λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, without further weight normalization. It keeps the teacher’s thinking prefix, uses the initial token weight c=0c=0, and clips weights to an upper bound of 1 and a lower bound that follows a cosine schedule from 0 to −1-1 over the first 50 steps. The initial token weight stays fixed throughout this clipping-bound schedule, which gradually permits negative weights. The OLMo coding run uses the same initial token weight and clipping schedule (Appendix C.3).

OPD2 compatibility settings. For the OPD2 compatibility experiment, the teacher pair is Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base. Our local implementation uses frozen-student TopK64 support and global token-mean reduction, with distillation coefficient λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 for both OPD2 and OPD2 + RAD. The RAD variant uses a cosine schedule for the initial token weight cc from 1 to 0, a clipping radius of 1 around cc, and weight learning rate γ=104​N1/N\gamma=10^{4}N_{1}/N. This schedule changes both the initial token weight and the clipping interval, moving the latter from [0,2][0,2] to [−1,1][-1,1]. Each step uses 64 actor prompts with eight responses each; RAD additionally uses 64 meta prompts with eight responses each. We compare OPD2 + RAD at step 100 with uniform OPD and OPD2 at step 200.

A.2 Implementation Details

Batch objective. Let ℬ={(𝒙i,𝒚i)}i\mathcal{B}=\{(\bm{x}_{i},\bm{y}_{i})\}_{i} be the current student rollout batch, with prefixes si,t=(𝒙i,yi,<t)s_{i,t}=(\bm{x}_{i},y_{i,<t}), and let NN be its number of valid response tokens. The temporary and committed updates use the normalized batch objective

L^D​(𝜽,𝒘,ℬ)=λN​∑i,twi,t​ℓD,t​(𝜽,𝒚i),\widehat{L}_{D}(\bm{\theta},\bm{w};\mathcal{B})=\frac{\lambda}{N}\sum_{i,t}w_{i,t}\ell_{D,t}(\bm{\theta};\bm{y}_{i}), (8)

where λ\lambda is the distillation coefficient. We keep the loss normalization fixed when differentiating with respect to the weights. The exact weight derivative is (λ/N)​Ii,t(\lambda/N)I_{i,t} (Equation 11). We update the weights using the scores Ii,tI_{i,t} directly with the separately specified weight learning rate γ\gamma in Equation 5. We also apply a detached token-level rollout/training importance correction clipped at 55, omitted from the notation. The weights are detached for the committed student update.

JVP backends. The flash_triton attention implementation combines a FlashAttention forward pass with a custom Triton kernel for the attention JVP (Algorithm 2). The Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 RAD experiments use this implementation to compute the model JVP on a temporary full student replica with its parameter direction. The olmo3_layer_streamed backend, used for OLMo3-7B-Instruct RAD coding, computes the model JVP one layer at a time: it gathers each parameter group and its direction, propagates activations and their tangents, and releases the gathered tensors after use. This execution strategy reduces parameter and direction storage while reusing the same flash_triton attention rule; Appendix H.1 gives the details.

A.3 Initial Token Weight Ablation

How does the initial token weight cc affect learning dynamics and final accuracy? In a four-run comparison, we study fixed c=0c=0, fixed c=1c=1, a cosine schedule from c=1c=1 to c=0c=0 over 100 updates, and fixed c=0c=0 with negative-weight warmup (Figure 6). The warmup keeps the upper clipping bound at 1 and lowers the lower bound from 0 to −1-1 with a cosine schedule through step 50, gradually permitting negative weights. All four runs use weight learning rate γ=104​N1/N\gamma=10^{4}N_{1}/N without further weight normalization. At step 100, fixed c=0c=0 reaches 32.71% mean accuracy without warmup and 31.20% with warmup, compared with 26.30% for fixed c=1c=1 and 27.45% for the cosine initialization schedule. Both zero-initialized variants outperform the other initialization choices at this checkpoint; fixed c=0c=0 without warmup leads the warmup variant by 1.51 percentage points in this single-seed comparison. The first three variants use [c−1,c+1][c-1,c+1], varying initialization and clipping bounds together; warmup changes only the lower bound while keeping c=0c=0.

Appendix B Extended Related Work

On-policy distillation for LLMs. Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a larger teacher to a smaller student (Buciluǎ et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015). For LLMs, teacher supervision can take the form of token-level probability distributions or generated text (Kim and Rush, 2016; Sanh et al., 2020). Off-policy distillation trains on fixed sequences, often generated by the teacher (Hsieh et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025). On-policy distillation instead queries the teacher on student-generated responses, exposing the student to supervision along its own trajectories and reducing the mismatch between training and inference (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). Self-distillation paradigm obtains supervision from the student itself, with privileged information such as verified solutions or environment feedback providing a stronger teacher context (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026).

Unifying distillation and RLVR. Several methods combine dense teacher supervision with verifiable task rewards. KDRL (Xu et al., 2025) jointly optimizes a GRPO reward objective and reverse-KL distillation, while RLAD (Zhang et al., 2026) incorporates teacher guidance into policy optimization through a likelihood ratio anchored to a mixture of the teacher and the previous student policy. RG-OPD (Akhondzadeh et al., 2026) uses agreement between verifier outcomes and teacher likelihoods to gate trajectory-level distillation. A related perspective connects OPD to KL-regularized reinforcement learning:  Yang et al. (2026) introduce a flexible reference model and scales the implicit reward derived from teacher probabilities, yielding the reward-extrapolation variant ExOPD. Our proposed method, RAD, uses task reward to determine how individual token-level distillation contributions should enter the student update.

Token-selective distillation. TIP (Xu et al., 2026) and DEAR (Xiao et al., 2026) select teacher supervision using uncertainty, teacher–student divergence, and reasoning structure. Reopold (Ko et al., 2026) combines token log-ratio rewards with clipping and entropy-guided sampling. Armandpour et al. (2026) diagnose token-level alignment between distillation and reward-improving directions in logit space and study oracle filtering of positively aligned tokens. RAD operationalizes reward-guided weighting during training: it differentiates a reward surrogate through the student optimizer and shared parameters to assign bounded, signed token weights. These weights can also reverse teacher contributions; our positive-only ablation supports the benefit of this additional flexibility. We compare RAD with representative reward-aware and token-selective baselines.

Bilevel reweighting. Learning example weights from a held-out objective is a standard use of bilevel optimization (Ren et al., 2018). Gradient similarity has also been used to adapt auxiliary losses toward a primary objective (Du et al., 2018). We apply this principle at token granularity in on-policy language-model distillation. The one-step approximation avoids solving the full inner problem or an implicit linear system (Liu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023).

Appendix D Preliminary Experiments on Agentic RL Settings

We apply RAD to an agentic software-engineering task. A Qwen3.5-4B 33 3 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B policy is trained on R2E-Gym (Jain et al., 2025b) with the OpenHands agent harness provided by R2E-Gym. Each episode presents a repository at a failing commit and lets the policy read, edit, and run code for up to 75 tool turns within a 65,536-token context, generating at most 8,192 tokens per turn with temperature 1, top-pp 1, and no top-kk truncation; the reward is the hidden test suite’s verdict on the final patch. Each update samples 32 tasks with eight attempts each and uses a constant learning rate of 10−610^{-6}. The teacher is Qwen3.6-27B.44 4 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B. The baselines train for one epoch on R2E-Gym, and RAD for half an epoch.

We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024; Chowdhury and others, 2024) with three rollouts for each of its 500 tasks under the training scaffold, sampling parameters, and context budget. Its repositories are disjoint from the training corpus. pass@1 is the mean resolved rate over all 1,500 attempts, and pass@3 is the fraction of tasks resolved by at least one of the three attempts.

RAD with negative-weight warmup reaches 50.5% pass@1 and 63.6% pass@3, the best of the five methods (Figure 9). It improves on GRPO by 5.9 points and on the strongest non-RAD baseline, RLAD, by 3.7 points, while training for half as many epochs.

Appendix H Custom Triton Kernel for Attention JVPs

In the flash_triton attention implementation, FlashAttention computes the attention output and row log-sum-exp during the model JVP in Equation 7, and a custom Triton rule propagates their directional derivatives. We describe scaled dot-product self-attention with zero dropout and no score softcapping. For one sequence and head,

S=QK⊤/d,P=softmax(S),O=PV,Li=log∑jexp(Si​j),S=QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d},\qquad P=\operatorname{softmax}(S),\qquad O=PV,\qquad L_{i}=\log\sum_{j}\exp(S_{ij}),

where Q,K,VQ,K,V are the queries, keys, and values, and dd is the head dimension. Softmax and log-sum-exp include only allowed keys in each row; masked probabilities are zero. Structural masks are fixed during differentiation. Dots denote directional derivatives induced by the parameter direction 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}, with Q˙,K˙,V˙\dot{Q},\dot{K},\dot{V} supplied by forward-mode differentiation through the preceding operations. The attention JVP is

S˙\displaystyle\dot{S} =(Q˙​K⊤+Q​K˙⊤)/d,\displaystyle=(\dot{Q}K^{\top}+Q\dot{K}^{\top})/\sqrt{d}, ai\displaystyle a_{i} =∑jPi​j​S˙i​j,\displaystyle=\sum_{j}P_{ij}\dot{S}_{ij},
O˙\displaystyle\dot{O} =P​V˙+(P⊙S˙)​V−a⊙O,\displaystyle=P\dot{V}+(P\odot\dot{S})V-a\odot O, L˙\displaystyle\dot{L} =a.\displaystyle=a. (14)

Here ⊙\odot is elementwise multiplication, with aa broadcast across each output row. The term −a⊙O-a\odot O accounts for differentiating the softmax normalizer. Reusing the saved O,LO,L, the kernel reconstructs probabilities one tile at a time and accumulates Equation 14.

Query blocks stay within sequence boundaries, so packed sequences cannot attend to one another. Causal, padding, and sliding-window masks use the same valid query–key pairs as the primal; grouped-query heads share their key/value tensors without explicitly repeating them. Our training launchers use 16-query blocks, with Triton autotuning key-block sizes of 16 or 32. Probability factors and tangent accumulators remain in FP32; the products with VV and V˙\dot{V} use tf32x3 tensor-core precision. The kernel stores O˙\dot{O} in the primal output’s dtype and L˙\dot{L} in FP32. It avoids storing full attention or attention-tangent matrices, while full-attention arithmetic remains quadratic in sequence length. The rule analytically differentiates the attention equations up to floating-point error.

H.1 Layer-Streamed JVP Execution

The olmo3_layer_streamed backend evaluates the embedding, decoder layers, final normalization, and output projection in sequence. For each parameter group, the FSDP executor gathers its parameters and the corresponding components of 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}, propagates both activations and activation tangents, and releases the gathered tensors after use. It can prefetch the next group, so gathered parameter and direction storage is bounded by the current and prefetched groups. Activation states are retained for a bounded set of microbatches at a time, with microbatch grouping synchronized across ranks to preserve the order of collective operations.

Within each OLMo decoder layer, the backend uses the same FlashAttention primal and Triton attention tangent as flash_triton (Algorithm 2), including the masks for full and sliding-window attention. Forward-mode differentiation propagates the chain-rule JVP through successive layers, reducing the memory needed for gathered parameters and their direction while retaining the token-score computation in Equation 7.
